paragraphs.text: X. A BOOK AGAINST SECUNDINUS.

I welcome the goodwill toward me that your letter shows. But as much as I ought to return the love of one who loves me, I am just as saddened that you have clung so stubbornly to false suspicions, partly against me and partly against truth itself, which cannot be changed. What you wrongly think about my mind I can easily disregard. What you think, though I do not recognize it in myself, can still happen in a human being. So even if you are mistaken about me, your mistake does not put me outside the human race, because what you believe of me can happen in a human mind, even if it has not happened in mine. There is therefore no need for me to work hard to rid you of this suspicion. Your hope does not depend on me, nor is it the case that you cannot be good unless I am. Think whatever you like of Augustine, so long as my conscience does not accuse me in the eyes of God. For as the apostle says, "To me it is a very small thing to be judged by you or by any human court." I will not, however, repay you in kind by daring to suppose anything bad about a mind of yours that I cannot see into. I do not say that you meant to wound me by stealth; I only think of you as much as your own words show. So although you have suspected no good of me, holding that I left the heresy of the Manichees out of a fleshly fear of some harm that might have come to me from your community, or out of desire for the honor I have gained in the Catholic Church, I do not in turn think badly of you. I believe your suspicion is well meant, and I take it that you wrote this not to accuse me but out of a desire to correct me. But if you would grant me the goodwill of believing me, since you are finding fault with the hidden recesses of my mind, which I certainly cannot bring out and display before your eyes, you would easily change your view of it and would no longer rashly assert what you do not know.

I admit it: I left the Manichees out of fear, but out of fear of the words spoken through the apostle Paul. "The Spirit," he says, "says plainly that in the last times some will depart from the faith, paying heed to seducing spirits and the teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, who forbid marriage and abstain from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving." Though these words may perhaps describe other heretics as well, they describe the Manichees above all, briefly and plainly. It was this fear, then, that tore me away from that community when, belatedly, I grew wiser than my childish understanding. I also admit that I burned with love of honor, and that this made me leave them, but it was the honor of which the same apostle says, "But glory and honor and peace to everyone who does good." Who will try to do good if he thinks that evil lies not in a changeable will but in an unchangeable nature? That is why the Lord himself said to those who thought they spoke good things although they were evil, "Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad." And to evil people who had already been changed into good the apostle says, "For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." But if you will not believe what I say about my own mind, think what you like; only take care what you think about truth itself. "Let no temptation seize you except what is human." It is a human error for you to believe that something happened in my mind which could have happened, even if it did not. But when you take for the truth a sacrilegious Persian fable, not only utterly false but utterly deceitful, woven and made up out of the foulest lies, and lies not about some human being but about the supreme God, this is not to be passed over in this way, nor is so great a death of the soul to be treated lightly. For here something can be done with you. About my own mind I can say nothing more than to ask you to believe me, and if you refuse, I find nothing further to do. It is not the same when you hold something false about the very light of minds, which rational minds behold the more calmly the purer they are. If you listen patiently, it can be shown to you how very far from the truth your view is. I cannot perceive what your eye perceives, nor you what mine does; on that matter we can only believe or disbelieve each other. But the visible form that lies before both our eyes we can point out to one another. So it is with the states of our minds: these are our own, so let us believe each other if we will, and if not, let us not. But the reasoning of truth, which is neither mine nor yours but is set before us both to contemplate, let us attend to together, with the fog of obstinacy laid aside and our minds made clear.

I will offer you no other evidence of the Manichaean error than your own letter. You write that you hold and give thanks to the ineffable and most sacred majesty and to his firstborn, the king of all lights, Jesus Christ. Tell me, of which lights is Jesus Christ king? Of those he made, or of those he begot? For we say that God the Father begot a Son equal to himself, but that through him he created, that is, founded and made, a lower creation, which is certainly not what he is who made it and through whom he made it. And so, since he made the ages through him, the apostle rightly called him the king of the ages, as one who is higher than what is lower, has the power to rule, and rules what needs to be ruled. But when you [?] call Christ the king of lights: if he begot them, why are they not equal to the one who begot them? And if you say they are equal, how is he their king, since a king must rule, and it is in no way possible for what is ruled to be equal to the one who rules it? If he did not beget these lights but made them, I ask what he made them from. If he propagated them from himself, why then are they lower? Why have they fallen short of their origin? And if not from himself, tell me from what. Or perhaps he neither made nor begot the lights over which he reigns? Then they have their own origin and nature, but surely a weaker one, so that they either allow themselves to be ruled, or desire to be ruled, by a more powerful neighbor. Do you not see that if this is so, then even leaving aside the race of darkness there are already two natures, one needing the other's help, but neither depending on the other as its source? You will surely reject this opinion, since it is utterly opposed to Mani, who tries to persuade people of two natures, not the king of lights and the lights that are ruled, but the kingdom of lights and the kingdom of darkness. So you will take refuge in saying that these lights were begotten. Then when I ask why they are weaker, you may try to argue that they are equal. But when I reply, "Then why are they ruled?" you will deny that they are ruled. To that I will answer, "Then why do they have a king?" At this point I see nothing left for your honest nature except to regret having put into your letter a door through which you yourself cannot get out. But even if you do regret it, and say that Mani should not be thought defeated just because you wrote something rather incautious in your letter, I will read you countless passages from Mani's books in which he speaks of a kingdom of light which he makes by nature the opposite of the kingdom of darkness; and not just a kingdom but kingdoms, since in that very letter of the ruinous Foundation, speaking of God the Father, he says, "with no one in his kingdoms established in need or in lowliness." Yet where there are kingdoms, who is so blind as not to see that kings cannot possibly be equal to those over whom they reign? What, then, if you will only pay attention, lies so near at hand and so befits the honesty of your heart as not to regret having put that phrase in your letter? For Jesus Christ is most truly king of lights that are in no way equal to him but subject to him, and he is the ruler of those blessed ones. Regret rather that you were a Manichee, since the truthful front of your letter has overturned all his deceitful contrivances at a single stroke, like a battering ram. For since Christ is king of lights, and he neither begot from himself lower beings to be king over, nor took over as neighbors to reign over beings that he neither begot nor made (lest there be two kinds of good, neither of which comes from the other, and yet one in need of the other, which strays from the path of truth), it remains that the lights over which he reigns, which are certainly good, God did not beget, since they are lower; did not usurp, as though they belonged to themselves; but made and founded.

If you want to ask what he made them from, and begin to imagine the assistance of a matter that he did not make himself, so that the Almighty would seem unable to make what he willed unless something he had not made helped him, you will again be caught in the inextricable fogs of error. But if, with a sober stroke of understanding, you apply most fittingly to that sublime and ineffable majesty the prophetic words, "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created," you will see how the Catholic faith can say that God made all things very good out of nothing. For if he made them out of something, it was either out of himself or not out of himself. If out of himself, then he did not make them but begot them. Why then did he beget lower beings? For unless they were lower, he could not be their king. If not out of himself, then certainly not out of something he did not make; otherwise he made them out of something not his own, and there was already a good that he had not made, from which he set up a kingdom for himself. If that is so, he ceases to be the creator of good works, since there was a good that he had not created; for he would not produce the lights over which he would reign out of some evil not his own. It follows, then, that even if he made them out of something, he made them out of something he had already made.

So it turns out that we must acknowledge that God made the first beginnings of the things to be created out of nothing. Unless perhaps, when you said that Jesus Christ is the firstborn of the ineffable and most sacred majesty, you meant it not with respect to his taking on of humanity, in which, as the apostle says and the Catholic faith believes, he deigned to have as brothers those called by adoption, so that he might be their firstborn, but rather wish him to be understood as firstborn with respect to the very excellence of his divinity, so that those lights in which he reigns are his brothers, not made by the Father through him but begotten by the Father after him, they being later-born and he firstborn, yet all of the Father's own and same substance. If you believe this, you first contradict the gospel, where he is also called only-begotten ("and we saw," it says, "his glory, as of the only-begotten of the Father"); this could in no way be said truly if his eternal power and divinity, in which he is consubstantial with the Father and exists before all creation, had brothers of the same substance. And so, since the divine scriptures testify that he is both only-begotten and firstborn (only-begotten because without brothers, firstborn because with brothers), you will find no way to understand both of him with respect to one and the same divine nature. But the Catholic faith, which distinguishes between Creator and creation, finds no difficulty in understanding these two names. It takes him as only-begotten according to what is written, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and as firstborn of all creation according to what the apostle says, "that he might be the firstborn among many brothers," whom the Father begot to share in his brotherhood not by equality of substance but by the adoption of grace. Read the scriptures, then: nowhere will you find it said of Christ that he is Son of God by adoption. But of us we read very often: "You have received the spirit of adoption as sons"; "awaiting the adoption, the redemption of our body"; "that we might receive the adoption of sons"; "he predestined us to adoption as sons"; "a holy nation, a people for adoption"; "he called you through our gospel to the adoption of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ"; and whatever other such passages come to mind as one recalls or reads them. It is one thing to be the only Son of God through the Father's excellence, and another to receive, through merciful grace, the power to become sons of God by believing in him. "He gave them," it says, "power to become sons of God." So they were not sons by nature, since they received the power to become so by believing in him whom, though he was his only Son, the Father did not spare but handed over for us all, so as to make him only-begotten with himself and firstborn toward us. Therefore, in that he is only-begotten, he was born not of flesh, not of blood, not of the will of a man nor of the will of the flesh, but of God; and in that he became firstborn among brothers in the Church, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. We too, insofar as we were by nature children of wrath, that is, children of punishment bound by the chain of mortality, were born of flesh and blood and of the will of the flesh, even though he created and formed us, he who without doubt orders and shapes all things, from the highest to the lowest, in measure and number and weight. But insofar as we have received the power to become sons of God, we too are born not of flesh and blood nor of the will of a man nor of the will of the flesh, but of God; not by a nature that makes us equal, but by a grace that adopts us.

Next, even if I were to grant that Christ Jesus is not the Father's only Son with respect to a divinity of the same substance, but has brothers born after him, of whom he is the firstborn, how can he be their king? I ask you, would you dare to say that he was born stronger because he was born earlier? You would surely be ashamed to think that. But you do not think so. Then what do you think? Calm your mind and make yourself willing to consider the truth without obstinacy. For I will ask this of you as well: how do you understand Jesus Christ to be firstborn in that divine, supremely good and eternal substance? Is he the first begotten in time, so that we are to understand that those of whom he is firstborn were born in that kingdom at a later time? We could not say by how many hours, days, months or years the one who came forth first is older, but we would still have to think of these generations as separated by some interval and span of time. Or are we to take him as firstborn not in time but in the very excellence of a surely higher majesty, by which he also merited to be king to his brothers the lights, as though begotten into a kind of preeminence? If you answer that he is prior to and older than his brothers in time, so as to argue that kingship over his brothers was conferred on him because he preceded them in birth and once existed when they did not yet exist, what are you saying, brother? Will you hurl your heart over this precipice of impiety, thinking that the changeableness of time befalls that divine and supreme nature, and believing that something exists there which did not exist before? Or, because lights had to go forth from there against the race of darkness, do you call those very goings-forth generations, and suppose that they took place in time so that the fighting could take place in time? Could not, then, a single light have sufficed to carry out that whole business of war by divine power? Or if many were needed, are we to think, in spiritual matters, that the way out was so narrow that they could not go out all at once, so that because one of the brothers went out first, he merited to be called firstborn and to become king over the rest? I do not want to pursue every point in detail, lest I burden too much a mind like yours, capable of seeing everything from a few things. So raise the eye of your mind and wipe away the mists of contention, and you will surely see that changes of place or of time, movements, advances, risings, settings, or any alterations whatever can occur only in a changeable creation. Yet unless that creation came from God, its maker and founder, the apostle would not have said, "And they worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever."

In this sentence there are two especially important points, and I ask you to consider them with me. First, if the creature were foreign to God, the apostle would not call God its Creator. Second, if Creator and creature were of one and the same substance, people would not be blamed for having served the creature rather than the Creator, since whichever one they served, they would not have departed from the same nature and substance. For just as no one can serve the Son without also serving the Father, since both are of one substance, so no one could serve the creature without serving the Creator, if both were of one substance. So if you now discern and understand, you would see that there is a very great difference between Creator and creature. And you must understand that the offspring of the Creator is not a creature; for if it were, it would not be lower but equal and of the same substance, and so whoever worshipped and served it would at the same time offer worship and service to its Creator and Father as well. But since the apostle rebukes and holds detestable those who worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, it is shown clearly enough that the one and the other are of different substances. For just as the Son cannot be seen, that is, understood, unless the Father is understood in him (for he himself says, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father too"), so the Son cannot be worshipped unless the Father is worshipped in him. And therefore, if the Son were a creature, he would not be worshipped without the Creator, nor would those be condemned who worshipped the creature rather than the Creator. So I think you now see that it does not suit you to call Jesus Christ the firstborn of the most hidden and ineffable majesty and the king of all lights unless you stop being a Manichee, so as to distinguish the creature from the Creator: so that Jesus Christ is both only-begotten, in that he is the Word of God, God with God, equally unchangeable and equally eternal, who did not think it robbery to be equal to God, and firstborn of all creation, in that in him were founded all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. You recognize, I think, the words of the apostle to the Colossians.

So when I ask you what the whole of creation was made from, creation that is good in its own kind yet lower than its Creator, and changeable while he remains unchangeable, you will find no answer unless you admit that it was made out of nothing. And that is why it can tend toward nothing when that creature sins, the part of it that can sin; not so as to become nothing, but so as to have less vigor and less firmness. For if you follow less vigor and less strength in your mind to its limit, what remains is nothing. So it loves vanity of its own accord when it abandons the solidity of truth and follows things of mere opinion, that is, changeable things. But when it then pays the penalty it deserves, it is subjected to vanity not of its own accord, as it was subjected in man when he sinned. For this is why the apostle says, "All creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly": because all creation is in man as well. For in man there is something invisible, his mind, and something visible, his body; and all creation is partly visible and partly invisible. Yet not all creation is in a beast, which has no intellectual mind. He says, indeed, that it was subjected in hope, because of the mercy of the one who sets it free through the forgiveness of sins and the adoption of grace. But if you refuse to admit that creation was made out of nothing by the Father through the Son in the goodness of the Holy Spirit, a Trinity that remains forever consubstantial, eternal and unchangeable, a creation good indeed, yet unequal to its Creator and changeable, you will certainly be forced to utter sacrilege: that God begot from himself something not equal to the one who begot it, something that could be subjected to vanity; or, if you call it equal, both will be changeable. What greater impiety is there than to believe and say such things, and to prefer, by a perverse opinion, to change God for the worse rather than, by corrected reasoning, to change oneself for the better? But if you are afraid to call God changeable, since that is indeed a great and most obvious impiety, and say instead that creation is unchangeable, so as to make it equal to the Creator and of one and the same substance, your own letter will answer you once again. For where does that soul come from which you place between the spirits, to which you say its nature gave victory from the beginning? You set before it a law and condition: if it acts as one with the spirit of the virtues, it will have eternal life with it and will possess the kingdom to which our Lord invites us; but if it begins to be drawn by the spirit of the vices and, after consenting, repents, it will have a fountain of pardon for these stains. When you recognize these words from your letter, you surely recognize at the same time that you have made the nature of the soul changeable. For what is it at one time to consent to the spirit of the vices and then again to repent, but to be changed now for the better, now for the worse? Most evident truth forced you to say this. For your own soul, if you wished to pretend otherwise, would press you to notice its changeableness; having been changed so many times since you were born, through various wishes, teachings, forgettings and consents, it would be its own witness and would look for no evidence from outside.

Unless perhaps you think it helps you to call the soul unchangeable, because you went on to say: "For it did not sin by its own will, but under another's leading; for it is led by its mixture with the flesh, not by its own will." Perhaps you want this statement understood to mean that the soul is unchangeable in its own nature but changeable when mixed with another nature, as though the question were why this is so, and not the fact that it is so. On that reasoning the bodies of Hector and Ajax, and indeed of all men and animals, would be called invulnerable, provided there were no blows or accidents that could inflict a wound on them. But surely the body of Achilles alone was called invulnerable, whether by poetic fiction or by some more hidden power of nature, because even when weapons rained down on it, it was not pierced; and in the one part where it could be pierced, it was certainly not invulnerable. So too, if the soul were unchangeable, it would be changed by mixture with nothing at all, just as a body that is invulnerable is wounded by the contact or attack of nothing at all. That is why we, who say that the Word of God cannot be defiled, are not afraid to believe that he was born of a virgin, even taking on mortal and vulnerable flesh, so as to teach us to despise death and every bodily hardship. You, on the other hand, believe in your impious perversity that the Son of God can be defiled, and so you are afraid to entrust him to flesh; and yet, while you declare that the nature of the soul is his substance, you claim that it is so mixed with flesh that you do not hesitate to think it has even been changed for the worse. Choose, then, what you want. Will you say or believe that God is changeable, so that you likewise believe a changeable offspring was begotten from the substance of a changeable Father? You surely sense how great an impiety that is. Or will you say that God is unchangeable, yet begot a changeable offspring from his own substance? You see that this is no less impious and absurd to say. Or do you rather confess God to be unchangeable in such a way that what he begot from his own substance is equally unchanged, and is equally the highest and most excellent good, and possesses supreme being in the same way, abiding inviolably; while the other, lesser goods, which we call creation, he made not from himself, for then they would be equal to him, but, since they are good, he made them, and since they are not equal, he made them from nothing? If you believe this, you will not be impious; you will forget the Persians and be one of us.

But, you say, the apostle declares: "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers", who turned aside by an impious will to the love of their own pride and honor, and begrudge pious souls their return. But here is the difference between your opinion and our faith. You think that these same princes arose from some nature of their own, which God neither begot nor made but which he had adjoining him as a neighbor from eternity; that they waged war against God, and that before good and evil were mixed they first inflicted on him the great evil of necessity, so that he was compelled to mix his own substance with them, to be afflicted and thrown into confusion, changed by error and wholly sunk in forgetfulness of itself, so that it needed a liberator, a corrector, a reformer, a teacher. You see how foolish and fabulous this is to say, and with what a crime of impiety it binds you. We, however, have been persuaded by the Christian faith that nothing is contrary to God, who supremely is, except what does not exist at all. Whatever exists in any way has from him who supremely is the fact that it exists in whatever way it does, and is good in its own kind; but some things exist more, others less. And so all the good things made by God the creator are ordered in fixed and allotted ranks: some by intervals of place and position, as all bodily things are; some by natural worth, as the soul is set above the body; some by the deserts of reward and punishment, as the soul is either raised to rest or subjected to pain. For this reason those princes against whom the apostle says we have our struggle suffer the punishment of their own sins first, in order to do harm. For no envious person injures another without first being a torment to himself. The stronger harm the weaker, since no one overcomes another except where he is more powerful. Yet these wicked princes are themselves weaker than they would be had they remained in their original state and in righteousness. It matters, however, in what respect one is stronger than another: whether in body, as horses are stronger than men; or by the nature of the soul, as the rational is stronger than the irrational; or by the disposition of the mind, as the just man is stronger than the unjust; or by rank of authority, as the emperor is stronger than the soldier or the provincial. And we believe that every power is given entirely by the supreme power of God; often it is even given to the worse over the better, that is, to the wicked over those who either already hold to righteousness or are striving to attain it. It is given for this purpose, that those who are tested through patience may be made manifest, either to themselves for hope or to others for imitation. "Knowing," says the apostle, "that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope." To this kind of contest belongs the faithful man's struggle against the principalities and powers of the apostate angels and against the spiritual forces of wickedness, when they receive power to tempt and he receives commandments to endure. So it happens that they win in the lower sphere and are beaten in the stronger: for the most part they overcome the weaker body and are overcome by the firmer mind. Against their force we fight with patience, against their snares with prudence, so that they neither bend us to ruinous consent by compulsion nor lead us astray by deceit. Now since the power and wisdom of God is he through whom all things were made, therefore among the things that were made, when higher things sink toward lower ones, which is where all sin and all that is called evil lies, force imitates power and deceit imitates wisdom; but when the things that had sunk run back and return, greatness of soul imitates power and learning imitates wisdom. God the Father himself is imitated by sinners through impious pride, and by the just through pious generosity. Finally, the Holy Spirit is imitated by the greed of the wicked and by the charity of the upright. Both, however, [?] withdraw from the imitation of God, from whom and through whom and in whom natures themselves were made, the one by a vicious imitation, the other by a praiseworthy one. Nor is it surprising that whenever those who are advancing and those who are falling away clash, the imitation of those falling away is overcome by the imitation of those advancing; for the former are thrown down headlong by exaltation, while the latter rise up by humility. And if it troubles you why those who are stronger in mind are weaker in body, it is no wonder that those set free by the forgiveness of sins should be trained by the mortality of the body, with whose immortality they will be crowned. For punishment is not easily escaped unless the one who is released from it has conquered by his merits. Hence the apostle says: "But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised [?] Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you." So the soul bears mortal flesh as the punishment of sin; but if, changed for the better, you do not live according to the mortal flesh, the soul changes that flesh too for the better and will deserve to have an immortal body. But this will be at the end, when death, the last enemy, will be destroyed, when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption, not by that fabulous globe of yours, but by the change of which he says: "We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed." For when he had stated, "and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed," he then went on to show what kind of change he meant, and said: "For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality." He was dealing with the question of the body of those who rise, which he had posed in these words: "But someone will say: How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?" So read that whole passage, intent on it with pious care and not troubled by obstinate contentiousness, and with your own understanding, God helping you and with no interpreter needed, you will find nothing other than what I am saying. Then bring your mind back to the subject we had set out to discuss, and see now, if you can, that I am not saying the righteous fight against nothing, but against those substances that fell away by not standing in the truth.

To fall away, however, is not yet to be nothing, but to tend toward nothing. For when things that exist more incline toward things that exist less, it is not the things toward which they incline that fall away, but the things that incline: they begin to exist less than they did, not so as to become the things toward which they inclined, but so as to be less according to their own kind. When the mind inclines toward the body, it does not become a body; yet by a defective appetite it becomes, in a way, bodily. So too a certain angelic loftiness, when it took greater delight in its own dominion within itself, turned its affection toward what is less, began to exist less than it had, and according to its rank tended toward nothing. For the less anything exists, the nearer it is to nothing. When these failings happen voluntarily, they are rightly blamed and called sins. And when these voluntary failings are followed by hardships, troubles, pains and adversities, all of which we suffer against our will, sins are surely rightly either punished by penalties or washed away by discipline. If you are willing to look at these things with a calm mind, you will certainly stop accusing natures and putting substances themselves on trial. And if you want a fuller and clearer treatment of this matter, read our three books entitled On Free Will, which you can find in Campania, at Nola, with Paulinus, the noble servant of God.

But now I must remember that I am answering your letter with a letter, even if a much longer one. That is precisely why I did not keep silent on other points: so that I would not be forced to say the same things everywhere. But I had promised to convince you from your own writings how false the things you have believed are, and how true the teaching of the Catholic faith is. Certainly not the whole of the difference between us lies in this, that you say evil is a substance, while we say that evil is not a substance but a turning away from what exists more toward what exists less. So listen to this point as well. In your letter you state about the soul that it is led to sin by its mixture with the flesh, not by its own will. And there, at once, I believe you saw that if this is so, every soul without exception must be rescued by almighty God and none at all ought to be condemned, since it would not sin by its will; and if that were established, the verdict that Mani thunders so terrifyingly about the punishment of souls, even those coming from the part of light, would be overturned. So, very watchfully, you added: "But if, once it has come to know itself, it consents to evil and does not arm itself against the enemy, it has sinned by its own will." It is good indeed that you at some point admit that the soul can sin by its own will. But to what evil, pray, does it sin by its own will if it consents? Surely to that which you say is a substance.

Now I already see three things, and you too, I think, see them with me. The soul that consents to evil and the evil itself to which it consents are two. The third is the consent itself; for you do not say that this is the soul, but that it belongs to the soul. Of these three, then, the soul, as you see, is a substance; and that evil to which the soul consents and so sins voluntarily is also, in your opinion, a substance. So I ask what this consent itself is: do you say it is a substance, or that it is in a substance? If you say it is a substance, you will now hold not two substances but three. Or do you still say two, because the consent of the soul, by which it consents to evil, is of the same substance as the soul itself? Then I ask whether this consent is evil or good. If it is good, the soul certainly does not sin when it consents to evil. Yet not only does the truth cry out, but you yourself write that it then sins by its will. This consent, therefore, is evil, and so the substance of the soul is evil too, if the consent is the substance of the soul and both are one substance. Do you see where you have been driven, so that you now declare the soul and that evil to be, not one good substance and the other evil, but two evil ones? Here perhaps you will try to attribute the blameworthy consent not to the soul that consents to evil, but to the evil itself to which it consents, so that in this way there can be two substances, one good and the other evil: the soul would be said to belong to the part of the good, while its consent by which it consented to evil, together with the evil itself to which it consents, would be placed on the other side, and both would be assigned to the evil substance, not to the soul. Who could rave more absurdly? For the soul does not consent if the consent is not its own; but it does consent; so the consent is its own. Furthermore, if the consent is its own, and this consent is evil, then this evil is its own. For if this evil too belongs to that evil to which the soul consents, that evil did not have this evil before the soul consented to it. What sort of good, then, is the soul, whose coming either doubles that evil or, to put it more mildly, increases it?

Next, if this consent, which is admittedly evil, is a substance, we find that it lies in the soul's power whether some evil substance exists or not, since this consent is in the soul's power. If it is not, then the soul does not consent by its own will; yet you said that because of this consent it sins by its own will. The soul therefore has it in its power, as I said, whether a certain evil substance exists or not. But what is a substance if not a nature? There will then be some nature that is neither natural to the soul, since it will not exist if the soul does not will it, nor natural to that evil to which the soul consents by its will; for you cannot say that what is brought into being there by another's will, that is, by the will of the soul, is natural evil belonging to the race of darkness. To what nature, then, will this nature, that is, this consent, be assigned, if it is a nature, since it is natural neither to the soul nor to the race of darkness, unless, arguing against Mani, you say there are not two natures but three? For even if at one time there were two, now, since this consent has arisen, they have certainly become three. And this third, born from the consenting soul and from the evil to which it consents, you will be forced to call the daughter, as it were, of both. But since it was born from two natures, one good and the other evil, I ask why something neutral was not born. For just as what is born of a horse and a donkey is neither horse nor donkey, so what is born of a good nature and an evil one, if it is itself a nature, ought to be neither good nor evil. Yet you admit that the consent is evil, since you say the soul sins by its own will when it consents to evil. Or do you perhaps think of the good nature and the evil nature as two sexes, male and female, so that, just as from a male and a female nothing neutral is born but either a male or a female, so you would contend that from good and evil there was born not some third thing that is neither good nor evil, but another evil? If that is so, where is that victorious nature of the soul? Has it been so set aside that another good was not born instead? And then, do you not see that you are now speaking of different sexes, not of natures? For if there were a difference of nature between good and evil, nothing could arise from the two but some third thing that could be neither good nor evil; or else the mixture itself would be sterile and no third substance would be produced from it. If from the animals I mentioned above nothing is born when they mate except a he-mule or a she-mule, which is neither the one nor the other, how much more should this have happened in so great and extreme a difference as that between good and evil? Or, if no new nature arose from their mixture, it would not be evil, even if it could not be good. It remains, then, that we cannot avoid such incredible ravings unless we admit that this consent, which is admittedly evil and blameworthy, is not a substance, and say that it is in some substance.

Next, let us inquire with the utmost care in what substance it is. Yet to whom is it not obvious that, just as persuasion occurs only in the one who persuades, so consent exists only in the nature that consents? When the soul consents to evil, then, the soul itself is a substance, but its consent is not a substance. You now see, I think, in what substance it is: you surely see that this consent is in the soul, and you do not doubt that this consent is a sin and therefore an evil. From this you now understand that there can be in a good substance, such as the soul, some evil that is not a substance, such as this consent, and from this evil the soul too is called evil. For a sinful soul is certainly evil, and it sins when it consents to evil. One and the same thing, then, the soul, is good insofar as it is a substance; but insofar as it has something evil that is not a substance, namely this consent, to that extent it is evil. For it has this consent not from advancing but from falling away. It falls away when it consents to evil, and begins to exist less, and therefore to be less strong, than it was while it stood firm in virtue, consenting to nothing; it becomes worse precisely to the degree that it turns from what supremely is toward what is less, so that it too exists less; and the less it exists, the nearer it comes to nothing. For whatever becomes less tends toward not existing at all; and although it does not reach that point, so as to perish entirely and be nothing, it is nevertheless clear that any falling away whatever is the beginning of perishing. Open, then, the eyes of your heart and see, if you can, that every substance of whatever kind is something good, and that the falling away of a substance is evil precisely because being a substance is good. Yet not every falling away is blameworthy, but only the voluntary one, by which the rational soul abandons its creator and turns its affection toward the things created below it; for this is what is called sin. The other failings, which are not voluntary, are either penal, so that sins may be punished under the governance and ordering of supreme justice, or they occur within the measures of the lowest things, so that what goes before gives way to what follows, and thus all temporal beauty runs its course in its own succession and after its own kind. A sentence runs its course as syllables die away and arise, as it were: they are drawn out through fixed intervals of time, and when their spans are complete, they depart in ordered succession to those that follow, until the whole utterance is brought to its end. Yet how long or short a syllable is to be, or in what form each letter keeps the moment of its place, lies not in the passing sounds themselves but in the control of the speaker, while the art that makes the sentence neither resounds in noises nor is rolled along and varied by times. In the same way, by the rising and setting, the departure and succession of temporal things over fixed and defined stretches, until it comes round to its appointed end, temporal beauty is woven together. This beauty is not evil simply because we can understand and admire better things in spiritual creatures; it has its own grace in its own kind, and to those who live well it intimates the supreme wisdom of God, hidden on high above all the bounds of time, which fashions and governs it.

Come now, consider whether that thing you called evil, by consenting to which the soul sins voluntarily, is some substance, or whether here too you cannot accuse a substance. For I ask what it is that entices the soul's consent: does that evil rush in [?], and is the soul said to consent because it is moved by some delight in it to enjoy it? If that is so, it does not follow that the thing should be called evil because it is wrongly loved. For if I show that something is loved wrongly where the fault lies with the lover and not with what is loved, you will surely admit that the beauty of a thing is not automatically faulty just because the consent of one who desires it slips into it faultily. How much this helps me will become clear later. But to show what I promised, what example should I choose, when I am surrounded by such an abundance of things? What, I say, should I choose rather than that which we praise as a heavenly creature, while you worship it as a portion of the creator himself? What among all visible things is more splendid than this sun? Yet if someone desires its light immoderately, he brings a war of quarrels upon his own eyes [?]; and if he gains some power by which he can accomplish what he craves, he tears down his neighbors' houses that stand next to his windows, so that the sun may flood the inner rooms of his house from a more open sky. Is that the fault of the sun, then, because this man so loved its light that he dared to prefer it to the light of justice, and, wishing to take in the light of his bodily eyes more abundantly into the dwelling of his body, shut the door of his heart and the eye of his mind against the light of equity? You see, then, that a good thing can be loved with a love that is not good. Therefore, when you call evil that by consenting to which the soul sins, I call it good in its own kind, but a good of such a kind that the soul, which is better, ought not to consent to it. For since the soul is superior to the body and has God superior to itself, then, although the nature of the body is good in its own order, the soul nevertheless sins, and by sinning becomes evil, if it gives to the inferior body the consent of love that it owes to God, who is superior to it.

But you may say that you do not call it blameworthy consent when a thing is loved that does nothing to win consent. You may say that the soul consents only when the thing it consents to persuades it to something or compels it to something, and that this thing is evil because it persuades or urges that some evil be committed. That is a second question, and it too must be dealt with in its proper order, and very soon. But first let us remember the first sin. It has, I think, been discussed enough, and it has become clear that something good in its own kind can be loved wrongly, and that when the lover is blamed the thing itself is not censured. What then? If a soul already sinful and corrupt through such love persuades another to the same sin, is not the soul that consents to the persuader corrupted by the same fault as the soul it follows? The first sin, then, is to prefer a creature, however good, to the Creator in one's love. The second is to try to bring another to do the same, whether by persuasion or by compulsion. For no one wants to lead another into depravity unless he has first been depraved himself. Those who sin want to lead others into sin either from foolish goodwill or from malicious envy. Who but a parent whose love is perverse advises his children to think no gain shameful and to get plenty of money wherever they can? He certainly does not hate them, and yet his advice is ruinous. He himself has already been corrupted by love of such things, though gold and silver are not evil, any more than the sun we spoke of above; still, the disordered lover of a good thing is at fault. In envy, when someone wants another to sin, he loves honour with immoderate pride and longs to excel in it and to surpass everyone else. Because he sees that honour is paid more fully and more truly to virtues, he wants others thrown down from the citadel of righteousness into the abyss of wickedness, so that he may not be outdone in it. This is how the devil tries to persuade or compel people to sin. But is honour itself at fault because the devil became wicked by loving it perversely and wickedly? Or is the devil's angelic substance, which God created, evil because it is a substance? No: he abandoned his love for God, turned too much to love of himself, and desired to appear God's equal, and so he was cast down by swollen pride. He is evil, then, not insofar as he is a substance. Because he is a substance that was made, he is evil insofar as he loved himself more than the one who made him. And he is evil because he is less than he would have been had he loved that which supremely is. Defection, therefore, is what is evil. Every defection tends away from what is toward not being, just as every advance tends from what is less toward being more. The highest honour, the kind that the devotion of religious people shows, is certainly owed to God. Whoever loves honour, therefore, imitates God. But humble souls wish to be honoured in him, the proud in preference to him. The humble, turned toward God, become higher than the unjust, while the exalted, set against God, become lower than the just. This is the dispensation of rewards and punishments: the former loved God above themselves, the latter loved themselves in place of God.

Now, I think, it is easy for you to understand from the very words of your letter, where you said that the soul sins by its will when it consents to evil. No evil is an evil nature or the love of an evil nature. Rather, since all natures are good in their own kind, evil is sin. Sin is done by the will of a soul when it loves the creature in place of the Creator, whether on its own impulse, when it is evil, or at another's persuasion, when it consents to evil. Even so, it becomes evil with punishments following, so that all things are ordered according to their deserts by the supremely good Creator, within a creature that is good but not supremely good, because he did not beget it from himself but made it out of nothing. You, however, have set up two natures. You hold that one of them is good and the other evil, or rather that one is the nature of good and the other the nature of evil, for an evil nature also comes from a good one through sin. Yet you admit that the nature you call good does evil by consenting to evil, that is, sins by its will. I, on the other hand, maintain that both are good, but that one of them does evil by persuading and the other does evil by consenting. Just as the consent of the one is not a nature, so neither is the persuasion of the other. And just as this one will remain good if it does not consent, keeping its nature whole, so that one will be the better if it does not persuade. If it did not itself commit the sin it does not urge, both would be equally whole and praiseworthy in their own kind. The one that both commits and persuades sins twice, and the other only once if it merely consents to doing evil. Still, they become evil by their sins; they are not evil by nature. Or if that nature is evil because of persuasion, then this one is evil because of consent. If it seems worse to you to persuade than to consent, let the one be bad and the other worse. But let there not be such partiality, such unjust favouritism in judging, that when both sin, though one more gravely and the other more lightly, one is called the nature of evil and the other the nature of good. Rather, either both are good, the one that sins less being the better, or both are evil, the one that sins more being the worse.

But where does the evil called sin come from, if there is no nature of evil? Tell me, where does that evil consent come from in the nature that you grant and proclaim to be good? Whatever undergoes being brought to consent to evil would certainly not undergo it unless it were able to undergo it. So I ask where it gets this very capacity to undergo, for it would be better if it did not have it. It is not, then, the nature of the supreme good, since something could be better than it. Next, if it has the power either to consent or not to consent, it does not consent because it is overcome. So I ask where it gets this evil consent, when no contrary nature compels it. But if it is compelled to consent, so that it is not in its power to do otherwise, then it does not sin by its will, as you were saying, since it does not consent by its will. And I ask further where it gets the capacity to be deceived, if it is deceived. Before it was deceived, unless there were something in it that made it able to undergo this, it would certainly never have undergone it. And in fact it consents only by its will; if it is compelled, it should be said to yield rather than to consent. But call it by whatever name you like. I put the question to you, a sharp and shrewd man with that Roman wit of yours you boast of: where does this nature of good get the capacity to undergo what it undergoes, so that it consents to evil? In a piece of wood, before it is broken, there is a brittleness; if it were not there, the wood could not be broken at all, and the wood is no less brittle if no one comes along to break it. In the same way I ask where this nature gets a certain brittleness or pliability before it is either broken by force or bent by persuasion into evil consent. Or if the brittleness was already there from the neighbourhood of evil, as bodies are often corrupted by the vapours of a nearby marsh, then it was already corruptible, if the pestilent contagion of that neighbourhood could corrupt it. So I ask: where does that corruptibility come from?

Please pay attention to what I am saying, and yield to the plain truth. I am not asking where corruption comes from. You will answer "from the corrupter," and you will insist that this corrupter is some prince or other of the race of darkness, so wrapped in the coverings of fables that one can hardly unwrap him and get hold of him. What I am asking is where corruptibility comes from, even before the corrupter arrived. If it had not existed, either no corrupter would have existed, or the approach of any corrupter at all would have done no harm. So find out where this corruptibility in the good nature came from, before it was corrupted by the contrary nature. Or, if you do not want to say that it is corrupted, then find out at least where this mutability came from before it was changed by the hostile attack. For a nature that turns from wise to foolish and forgets itself certainly does change for the worse. You yourself used these words, saying: "if, when it has come to know itself, it consents to evil." So it is changed for the worse when it forgets itself, so that it must be reminded in order to know itself again. Yet it could not have been changed in any way unless it was changeable before it was changed. When, then, you have found where this mutability came from in the substance of the highest good, before there was any mixture of good and evil, you will surely stop asking me where evil comes from. And yet in the nature of the highest good, if you think about it rightly, no mutability of time can be found at all, either arising from itself or from the approach of anything else. So, in the nature that Mani invents and judges to be supremely good, or even persuades his believers to be so, ask and answer, if you can: where does this mutability come from, which was not produced but laid bare when the delay [?] came? For it could not have been changed even by an enemy if it could not be changed at all. Since it could be changed, it showed that it had not been made unchangeable. So when this mutability is believed to exist in the substance of the highest good, that is, in the substance of God, you can see, unless you are contentious, what great folly lies in this blasphemy. But when something of this kind is said about a creature, which God neither begot nor brought forth from his own substance but made from nothing, we are not dealing with the highest good. We are dealing with a good of such a kind that it could not have been established except by the highest good, who is God. For God, who is supremely and unchangeably good, made all things good. They are not supremely or unchangeably good, but they are good all the same, from the angels of heaven down to the lowliest beasts and plants of the earth, all set in their fitting places according to the dignity of each one's nature. Among these, the rational creature keeps its nature safe in God's eternity, truth and love when it clings with the obedience of love to God, its creator, that is, its maker and founder. But when it deserts him through stubborn disobedience, it entangles itself in sins through its free will, and through his just judgment it is made wretched by punishment. And this is the whole of evil: partly what it does unjustly, partly what it justly suffers. Do not ask me where this comes from, since you have already answered yourself when you said that when the soul has come to know itself, if it consents to evil, it sins by its own will. There, you see, is where evil comes from: from one's own will. This is not a nature but a fault, and for that very reason it is contrary to nature. It certainly harms nature by depriving it of the good by which it could have been happy if it had been unwilling to sin. You think that this will to sin is moved in the soul only by another evil, which you believe to be a nature that God did not make, and you contend that the soul is the nature of God. And so, if this nature of evil, whatever it is, produces this will in the soul by persuading it to sin, God is defeated and thrown down into sin.

See how great the impiety is, how wicked and horrible the blasphemies that you refuse to strip off! You place in a nature that God did not make life, sense, speech, measure, form, order and countless other goods. And you place in God's own nature, before any mixture with evil, that very mutability by which it could be captured and because of which it was forced to be afraid, "seeing that great ruin and devastation threatened his holy worlds unless he set against it some outstanding and glorious deity, mighty in power." And what is all this for, except that this nature and substance of God should hold the enemy entangled and subdued? Sinning, it endures him, and bound, it does not wholly escape. Once purged, it holds him conquered, and once condemned, it keeps him shut in. You have indeed found a splendid excuse in your God, the necessity of war. You offer it against the question put to you to answer: what would the race of darkness have done to God if he had been unwilling to fight it? If you say that it would have done him some harm, you will be admitting that God is corruptible and can be violated. If you say that it could not have harmed him, you will be asked: why, then, did he fight? Why did he hand over his own substance to enemies, to be corrupted, violated and forced into every sin? You have never been able to find a way out of this dilemma.

You think you have found something great and safe when you answer by saying: "It is a great iniquity to covet what belongs to another, and God would have given his assent to this iniquity if he had been unwilling to conquer the race that had dared to do it." This answer would have some sort of color of justice if, at least in that war, the nature of your God had kept itself whole and unpolluted, and had done nothing wicked, whether forced or seduced, while mixed with the hostile members. But you say that it consented as a captive to such great crimes and outrages. Finally, you claim that it cannot be wholly purged of that monstrous impiety by which it even became an enemy of the holy light of which it is a portion, and for this reason you believe that the eternal punishments of that horrible globe are deservedly paid back to it. Given all this, who does not see how much better it would have been to leave the hostile enemy in its own iniquity, attempting empty schemes, than to hand over to it a part of God, whose strength it would drain and whose corrupted beauty it would join to its own iniquity? Who is so blinded by such obstinacy as not to perceive, not to notice, how much smaller an iniquity it would have been for the race of darkness to try in vain to invade a nature not its own, than for God to hand over his own nature to be invaded, forced into iniquity, and in some part even condemned to punishment? Is this, then, what it means to refuse to consent to iniquity: to commit so vast an iniquity without any necessity? Or was there a necessity? Mani himself was not ashamed to say so, but you are ashamed to. For he says that God saw that great ruin and devastation threatened his holy worlds unless he set against it some outstanding deity, mighty in power. You, of course, think that you reason more sharply than that. But if you were to say that God fought out of necessity, so that the race of darkness would not harm him, you would be calling God violable and corruptible, since something could have harmed him if he had been unwilling to fight. So drive out and expel from your hearts and from your faith even that battle itself, and that whole fable woven of horrifying, impious and utterly unclean blasphemies. At long last, anathematize and condemn it. For what sort of thing is this, I ask you? As was said before, you are not afraid to call that nature, God, violable and corruptible. And if the nature of your God could not exercise the strength that would have kept it from being captured, could it not at least keep its righteousness while captive? Daniel could do that, and you dared to mock his lions. Compelled by no terror, he did not [?] consent, in his piety, to the iniquity of those who had led him captive. Even in the condition of bodily servitude he did not lose the fairness and freedom of a patient and wise mind. The nature of God, however, was led captive, was made unjust, cannot be wholly purged, and is forced to be condemned at the end. If it knew from eternity that this evil would befall it, then no divinity was owed to it by right of itself [?]. You also said that the lands or regions of the kingdom of light and of the race of darkness, which bordered on each other, are beyond description. Mani tells of them in a way that people of sound understanding can only laugh at. You further said that Christ calls these regions the right and the left. But we know that when Christ speaks of the right and the left, he wants these words understood not as bodily things, but as the blessedness and misery of each person according to their merit. Your carnal thinking, however, is so far from leaving bodily places behind that you say this visible sun is both God and part of God, though it is a bodily thing and cannot be contained except in a bodily place. But it is foolish to argue with you about these things. For what incorporeal thing will you be able to understand, when you do not yet believe that God is incorruptible?

But of course, as a good friend, you kindly scold me for leaving the Manichees and turning to the books of the Jews. Yet it is these very books that choke your error and deceit. In them Christ was foretold as the truth of God has shown him to be, not as the empty imagination of Mani made him up. But you, the most urbane of men, attack the ancient Scripture because it is written in the prophet: "And make children of fornication, for the land will commit fornication away from the Lord," even though you hear in the Gospel: "Prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of heaven." I know where your indignation comes from. What displeases you is not so much the fornicating woman in her fornication as the fact that she was changed into a wife and turned to the chastity of marriage. There, you believe, your God is bound with tighter chains of flesh when children are conceived. You think that prostitutes spare him, because they take pains not to conceive, so that, free of the duty of bearing children, they can serve their lust. For among you a woman's conception is a prison and a chain for God. That is also why you dislike the words "The two shall be in one flesh," although the apostle commends this as a great mystery in Christ and the holy Church. That is why you dislike "Increase and multiply": you fear that the prison-houses of your God will multiply. But I confess that I learned in the Catholic Church about the soul and the body, one of which is set over [?] the other and the other subject to it. I learned that the good of the soul and the goods of the body alike come only from the supreme good, from whom come all good things, whether great or small, heavenly or earthly, spiritual or bodily, temporal or eternal. Nor are the lesser goods to be condemned because the greater are to be preferred.

You also count "Kill and eat" among the things to be blamed, but this too is set down in a spiritual sense in the Acts of the Apostles. Yet even in the bodily sense, food is not blameworthy; luxury is. You in particular, who abstain from meat even in the bodily sense, ought to have been glad to accept this saying. Then you could kill flesh, break open the prisons, and let your God escape from his miserable confinement. And if any remnants of him were left there, you could purify them by eating them in the workshop of your belly. You mock me for having grieved over Sarah's barrenness. I certainly did not grieve over it, since that barrenness was itself prophetic. But your sacrilegious fables would have you grieve not over Sarah's barrenness but over fertility, since every woman's fertility is a harsh calamity for God. So it is no wonder that what was foretold about such people is fulfilled most of all in you: "forbidding marriage." For you detest marriage even more than sexual intercourse, because in marriage intercourse for the sake of having children is not a vice but a duty. Holy men and women who live in continence are exempt from this duty. This is not because they shunned it as an evil, but because they chose something better. With fathers and mothers such as Abraham and Sarah, however, the duty of marriage itself must be judged not by ordinary human partnership but by God's plan. Since Christ had to come in the flesh, Sarah's marriage served the propagation of that same flesh which Mary's virginity also served.

The same applies to the words you mocked in a laudable ignorance: "Put your hand under my thigh." Abraham said this to his servant when he required him to swear an oath: "Put your hand under my thigh," he said, "and swear by the God of heaven." The servant swore in obedience, but Abraham, in giving the command, was prophesying that the God of heaven would come in the flesh that would descend from that thigh. You reject this, you detest it, you find it abominable, you chaste and clean men. For the Son of God, whom no contact with flesh could have changed, you dread a single virgin's womb. Yet you entangle the nature of your own God, changed and polluted, in the wombs of all females, not only of human beings but of animals too. So you shudder at the one thigh of a patriarch. But what thighs can you find, not of prophets but of any prostitute at all, where you ought not to swear by your God, so shamefully shackled there? Perhaps it is not chastity that keeps you from touching a member of the human body. Perhaps you are ashamed to swear by a God so shamefully bound and held captive there in such disfigurement. Using the name "pancarpus," the kind of show usually staged at the public games, you attack Noah's ark because of the beasts of every kind that were in it. Yet through every kind of animal that ark prefigured the Church that was to come from all nations. I congratulate you here for choosing a fitting word, though you did so without noticing or without knowing it: for pankarpos means "every fruit," and this is spiritually true of the Church. And you do not consider how much happier Noah was than your God. Noah and his family were among those wild beasts; he went in unharmed and came out unharmed. Your God was torn apart and devoured by the bestial fury of the race of darkness. So he became not a pancarpus but plainly a camparcus [?], since he was torn to pieces by every kind of savagery. You ridicule Jacob's wrestling with the angel, in which Israel's struggle with the flesh of Christ to come was prophetically foreshadowed. But however you understand it, how much better it would be for your God to wrestle with a man than to be conquered, taken captive and torn apart by a race of demons! You falsely accuse Abraham of selling his wife's chastity. He did not lie in calling her his sister. Out of human caution he kept quiet about her being his wife, and he entrusted the protection of her chastity to his God. If he had not done what he could do himself, he would have been judged guilty of tempting God, not of trusting in God. Yet you take no notice of your own God, who gave not his wife but his own members to his enemies to be polluted, corrupted and defiled. He did not even sell them; he gave them away for nothing. Surely, if it were possible, you would wish that the glorious nature of your God might return to him from his enemies as undefiled as Sarah was returned undefiled to her husband.

You praise my former character and pursuits, and you ask who suddenly changed me. Then, by a roundabout phrase, you mention the ancient enemy of all the faithful, of the saints, and of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and you clearly mean the devil. What answer should I give you about my change? If I did not believe that it was a change for the better, would I have detested and condemned your error and turned to the Catholic Church and faith? Did I do right? That is, was I changed from bad to good? You answer this question for me yourself with the very word you used: my "change." If my soul were the nature of God, as you say, it could not be changed at all, whether for the better, as I trust, or for the worse, as you claim. It could not be changed by itself or by any outside force. So I left that error and chose the faith in which the nature of God is devoutly believed to be wholly unchangeable, so that this may be wisely understood. My change, then, displeases only those who are displeased by an unchangeable God. The devil is indeed the adversary of the saints. This is not because he rises against them as an enemy from an opposing principle of another nature. It is because he envies them the heavenly honor from which he himself was cast down. Having been changed himself, he works to change others. As you describe him in that long-winded Persian fable, if he changes others without being changed himself, he is surely greater than they are and their conqueror. But if, as you claim, he [?] the holy light, then he is not God's enemy but God's friend. And is he better than those he deceives, when he makes them enemies of the holy light to which he himself is a friend? For this is why Mani says that souls are to be condemned to eternal punishment in that horrible globe: they allowed themselves to stray from their former shining nature and so became enemies of the light. Yet he maintains that the mind of the race of darkness itself burned with desire to keep the light within it and created the bodies of animals. Take care, then, to rescue yourself from these utterly empty and sacrilegious fictions, and to be changed for the better with the help of him who is changed neither for the better nor for the worse.

"We escaped," he says, "because we followed a spiritual Savior. For the enemy's daring broke out so far that, if our Lord had been made of flesh, all our hope would have been cut off." If you say this because you do not believe that Christ had flesh, you ought not to put your hope in Mani. You admit that he was begotten of a man and a woman like other people and lived in the flesh. Why, then, do you put so much hope in him? For in this very letter of yours, while trying to frighten me, you said: "Who will be your advocate before the just tribunal of the Judge, when you begin to be convicted of your words and deeds by your own testimony? The Persian whom you accused will not be there. Apart from him, who will comfort you as you weep? Who will save the man from Carthage?" So you said that apart from Mani there can be no comforter and no savior. How, then, could you say, when you were discussing Christ's sufferings, that you escaped because you followed a spiritual Savior, meaning that the enemy could not kill him if he had been in the flesh? The enemy found flesh in your Mani and killed him, so that he could no longer be your savior. How, then, can you say, "Apart from him, who will comfort you as you weep? Who will save the man from Carthage?" You see what it means to be in heresy, following doctrines of demons in the hypocrisy of liars. You want Mani to be truthful at the cost of making Christ a deceiver. Christ showed his flesh, his death and his resurrection, and finally the places of the wounds and the nails, to his doubting disciples. If he did all this deceitfully and falsely, then Mani told the truth about Christ. But if Christ showed true flesh, and therefore a true death, a true resurrection and true scars, then Mani lied about Christ. So the difference between you and me in this matter is this. You have chosen to believe that Mani is truthful by believing that Christ is a deceiver. I have chosen to believe that Mani lied about Christ, as he lied about other things, rather than that Christ lied about anything at all. How much less would Christ lie about the thing on which he placed the greatest hope of believers, namely his passion and resurrection! After what was thought to be his death, Christ appeared to his disciples while they hesitated and thought they were seeing a spirit, and he said: "Touch my hands and feet and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." And to one of them who refused to believe he said: "Put your fingers into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing." Whoever says that Christ showed all this not truthfully but falsely is not a preacher of Christ but his accuser. "But," you say, "Mani preaches Christ and calls himself his apostle." That is all the more reason to detest him and flee from him. If he said these things to accuse Christ, he could at least boast that he loved the truth by exposing another's falsehood. As it is, he unknowingly and carelessly gives himself away, and to anyone who looks closely he shows clearly enough what he does and what he loves, since he praises and preaches one who lies. So flee from so great a plague, my friend. Mani would like to make you a believer by deceiving you, though that cannot happen, just as he would have it appear that Christ made a believer of the disciple to whom he said: "Put your fingers into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing." As the sweetest truth understands it, what else did Christ say to the disciple but this: "Touch what I bear, touch what I have borne. Touch true flesh, touch the marks of true wounds, touch the true places of the nails, and by believing what is true, do not be unbelieving but believing"? But as the sacrilegious folly of Mani senselessly understands it, what else did Christ say to the disciple but this: "Touch what I pretend, touch what I falsify. Touch false flesh, touch the deceptive places of false wounds, and do not be unbelieving toward my lying members, so that by believing what is false you may be a believer"? Such are the believers of Mani, the master of every doctrine of lying demons.

Flee these things, I beg you. Do not let the appearance of being few deceive you because the Lord himself said that the narrow way belongs to few. You want to be among the few, but among the worst. It is true that few people are innocent in every way. But among the guilty themselves, murderers are fewer than thieves, and those who commit incest are fewer than adulterers. Even the fables and histories of the ancients have fewer Medeas and Phaedras than women guilty of other crimes and outrages, and fewer men like Ochus and Busiris than men guilty of other impieties and wicked deeds. So consider whether, among you, it is the sheer horror of your impiety that makes you few. The things read, said and believed there are such that the wonder is that anyone at all, rather than only a few, should rush into that error or remain in it. The fewness of the saints, whose way is narrow, is measured against the great number of sinners. These few are hidden among a far larger quantity of chaff, but they are now being gathered and threshed on the very threshing floor of the Catholic Church, and at the end they will be winnowed and cleansed. You must come over to that Church if you truly desire to be faithful. Otherwise, by trusting in falsehoods you will "feed the winds," as Scripture says; that is, you will become food for unclean spirits. You mention the apostle Paul. He counted certain things as loss and dung in order to gain Christ, but these things were not, as you [?] think, the Scriptures of the Old Testament and the whole prophetic plan of words and deeds. They were the fleshly distinction of his Jewish descent; the zeal, which inflamed him as if it were praiseworthy, to persecute Christians on behalf of the synagogues of his ancestral people, who had gone astray and did not recognize Christ; and the righteousness that comes from the law, in which the Jews proudly boast because they do not understand the grace of God in it. If Paul did this, how much more ought you to cast away those writings! They are full of unspeakable blasphemies. In them the nature of truth, the nature of the supreme good, the nature of God is described as changeable again and again, conquered again and again, corrupted again and again, partly defiled beyond remedy, and in the end condemned by the truth itself. You should throw them away not as dung but as poison. Put an end to the dispute and come over to the Catholic Church and faith, which was foretold so long before and was revealed in its own time!

I say this to you because your mind is neither the nature of evil, which does not exist at all, nor the nature of God. If it were God's nature, I would be speaking in vain to something unchangeable. But it has been changed by deserting God, and that very change is evil. So let it be changed again by turning to the unchangeable good, with the help of that unchangeable good itself, and such a change will be its deliverance from evil. Perhaps you reject this warning and go on believing in two natures. One, the changeable nature of good, could consent to injustice when mixed with evil. The other, the unchangeable nature of evil, could not consent to justice even when mixed with good. If so, you will go on babbling the shameful fable I have just described, which sows hateful and foul blasphemies into the fornication of itching ears. Then you will belong to the flock of those of whom it was foretold: "The time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but, having itching ears, they will heap up teachers for themselves to suit their own desires. They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to fables." But if you wisely accept this warning and turn to the unchangeable God, a praiseworthy change will make you one of those of whom the apostle says: "You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." This could not be said of the nature of God, because it was never evil and never deserved the name of darkness. Nor could it be said of the nature of evil, for if such a nature existed, it could never be changed and become light. But it was rightly and truly said of the nature that is not unchangeable. When it deserts the unchangeable light by which it was made, it becomes dark in itself. When it turns to that light, it becomes light, not in itself but in the Lord. For it does not shine of itself, since it is not the true light. It shines because it is lit by him of whom it was said: "That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world." Believe this, understand this, hold on to this, if you want to be good by sharing in the unchangeable good. You cannot be good through yourself. If you were good unchangeably, you could never lose that goodness, and if you were not good unchangeably, you could not receive it back by your own power.
